articles.title: The Trial That Made The Supreme Court Untouchable
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

Who is the only Supreme Court justice who has ever been impeached by the House?

Hint: A signer of the Declaration of Independence appointed by George Washington, he was hauled before the Senate on eight articles for conduct his political enemies called nakedly partisan. He was acquitted — an outcome long credited with establishing that a justice can’t be removed simply for rulings the ruling party dislikes.

See the answer on the next page.

articles.title: The Three Pillars Of Business Development For Lawyers
articles.content:
在与律师精英（The Lawyer’s Edge）创始人兼CEO艾丽丝·霍尔茨曼（Elise Holtzman）的最近对话中，史蒂夫·弗雷津（Steve Fretzin）直击法律界最顽固的一个迷思：认为开发客户是天生的能力，要么有，要么没有。

霍尔茨曼提出了完全相反的观点：业务开发是一项可学习的技能。就像任何有价值的技能一样，它需要正确的心态、可重复的流程，以及愿意组建一个团队来帮助你超越个人能力的限制。

**挑战意味着你正在成功**
对话中最解放人心的想法是霍尔茨曼对成长过程中伴随的挑战的重新定义。大多数律师在某个阶段都会遇到困境，但往往误以为这是自己做错了什么，或者不具备相应的能力。然而，真正的挑战恰恰证明了你正在朝着正确的方向前进。

**弗雷津的“三个P”**
弗雷津在对话中补充了自己的“三个P”框架，与霍尔茨曼的“三大支柱”相辅相成：
1. **明确目标**（Purpose）：清楚你想服务的客户群体。
2. **制定计划**（Plan）：制定可执行的行动方案。
3. **持之以恒**（Persistence）：坚持执行并进行调整。

**真正的开发客户如何扩展**
对话中最实用的部分之一是关于如何在建立了稳固的客户群体后，进一步扩大业务而不必亲力亲为。霍尔茨曼介绍了“赞助”（Sponsorship）的概念，这是一种更主动、更互惠的导师关系，帮助律师更好地发展。

**从随机行动到真正策略**
整个对话的核心是从零散的努力转向有组织的、可扩展的客户开发。抱着希望做生意不是策略，参加同一场会议和等待电话铃声也不是策略。真正有效的是明确目标客户、在正确的场所提高能见度、制定可遵循的流程，并培养一个与你共同成长的团队。

正确的业务开发不像推销，更像建立一种能够复利增长的事业，而这种能力对任何愿意为它付诸行动的律师来说都是可以掌握的。

**关于史蒂夫·弗雷津**
史蒂夫·弗雷津是五次畅销书作家，主持《成为那位律师》（BE THAT LAWYER）和《未来创客》（Future Rainmakers）播客，也是一位专门服务律师的业务开发教练。在过去18年中，他帮助律师通过“不卖的销售”（Sales-Free Selling™）方法建立强大的客户群，无需推销、演示或追逐。他的客户往往成为顶尖的开发客户者，并将他们的增长归功于他的教练和系统。史蒂夫可通过电子邮件steve@fretzin.com或网站www.bethatlawyer.com联系，也可在LinkedIn添加他：https://www.linkedin.com/in/stevefretzin。他的全新社群“成为那位律师社区”（BE THAT LAWYER Community）正在改变律师们发展那些法律学校从未教授的技能的方式。了解更多请访问www.bethatlawyer.com/community。
articles.summary:
In a recent conversation with Elise Holtzman, founder and CEO of The Lawyer’s Edge, Steve Fretzin tackled one of the most persistent myths in the legal profession: that rainmaking is something you’re either born with or you’re not. 

What Elise laid out was the opposite. Business development is a learnable skill, and like any skill worth having, it requires the right mindset, a repeatable process, and the willingness to build a team that helps you scale beyond what you can do alone. 

New Challenges Mean You’re Succeeding 

One of the most freeing ideas from the episode was the reframe Elise offered around the challenges that come with growth.

Most lawyers hit a wall at some point and read it as a sign they’re doing something wrong, or that they’re not built for this. 

The Three Ps 

Steve brought his own framework into the conversation to complement Elise’s “three pillars.”

Here, Steve shares his the “three Ps” of business development. 

How Real Rainmakers Scale

The third thread from the episode was one of the most practical: what happens when you’ve built a strong book of business and you want it to grow further without doing everything yourself? 

Elise described the concept of sponsorship, a more intentional and mutual form of mentorship.

From Random Acts of Marketing to a Real Strategy 

The through line across this entire episode is the shift from scattered effort to focused, scalable rainmaking. Hope is not a strategy. Showing up to the same conferences and waiting for the phone to ring is not a strategy. What works is clarity on who you’re trying to reach, visibility in the right places, a process you can actually follow, and a team that grows alongside you. 

Business development done right doesn’t feel like selling. It feels like building something that compounds, and it’s available to any lawyer willing to treat it like the learnable skill it is.

Steve Fretzin is a five-time bestselling author, host of the BE THAT LAWYER and Future Rainmakers podcasts, and a business development coach who works exclusively with attorneys. For more than 18 years, he has helped lawyers build strong books of business without selling, pitching, or chasing, using his proven Sales-Free Selling™ approach. His clients consistently become top rainmakers and credit his coaching and systems for driving meaningful, measurable growth. Steve can be reached directly at steve@fretzin.com, or through his website at www.bethatlawyer.com. Connect with him on LinkedIn at https://www.linkedin.com/in/stevefretzin. His ALL NEW BE THAT LAWYER Community is changing how lawyers develop the skills never taught in law school. Learn more at www.bethatlawyer.com/community.

articles.title: Judges Should Not Make Lawyers Handwrite Orders After Oral Argument
articles.content:
我职业生涯中遇到的最奇怪的实践之一，是法官在庭审中裁定动议后，要求律师手写一份订单记录法院的裁决。虽然并非所有法院都这样做，许多法官或是亲自准备订单，或是要求各方在庭审后提交草案，但我确实见过法官宣布裁决后，要求律师当场甚至在法庭上手写订单供法官签字的情况。

我理解法官采取这种做法的原因。法院工作繁忙，让律师记录刚刚发生的事情可能比要求法院人员准备订单更有效率。此外，律师显然了解案件的问题，应该能够将简单的裁决写成文字。不过，法官通常应避免这种做法，因为律师有对立利益，而庭审后立即准备的手写订单可能会造成不必要的混乱。

最大的问题是，律师可能对法官的实际裁决存在分歧。口头裁决通常没有书面裁决那么精确。法官可能讨论几个问题，解释初步想法，然后宣布裁决，但未具体说明实施该裁决所需的所有细节。一场庭审后，各方可能对具体获得了什么救济和未来各方的义务有不同的理解。

当律师被要求写订单时，这种情况让律师处于尴尬的境地。律师自然希望起草有利于其客户的文字。当然，律师有道德义务，不应故意误述法官的裁决。但关于如何将口头裁决转化为文字，可能有相当大的合理分歧。一位律师可能认为法官的意图是广泛的指令，而另一位律师可能认为裁决狭窄得多。

我曾经处理过这样的情况：法官在庭审中裁定动议后，要求律师手写记录裁决。几乎立刻，律师们就订单中应出现的文字产生了分歧。尽管大家刚刚听到的是同一裁决，但各方对法官的意图却有不同的看法。裁决不仅没有结束争议，反而在如何描述裁决本身上创造了新的争议。

手写订单还可能造成其他问题。律师通常在庭审中专注于为客户辩护，而不是完美记录法官说的每一句话。律师可能在思考法官的提问、对方的论点，或是庭审结束前需要处理的问题。因此，几分钟后就要求律师重建裁决的精确范围，很可能会导致错误。

此外，重要的司法指令以法庭内匆忙的手写方式记录，也不是理想的做法。根据情况，订单可能会影响调查义务、期限、金钱支付、禁令以及许多其他重要权利。律师和客户可能需要在几个月甚至几年后依赖订单的精确用语。当有一份清楚的文件准确反映法院的意图时，所有人都会受益。

当然，法官并不需要亲自起草每一份订单。在许多情况下，法官在庭审后要求律师提交订单草案是合理的。这样可以给各方时间审查文字、必要时查阅记录，并在订单生效前识别分歧。然后法官可以解决任何用语争议，签署一份准确反映法院裁决的文件。

法官也可以在记录中口头宣布订单的精确条款，或是让法院工作人员在裁决简单时准备一份简短订单。这些方法中的任何一种都可以减少单方由于恰巧拿着笔而对用语产生过大影响的可能性。

律师已经有足够多的争论事项。他们不应在法庭上因法官五分钟前的意思争论而再次陷入谈判。当法院发布裁决时，如果订单清晰、深思熟虑并无可置疑地反映法官的裁决，所有人都会受益。因此，法官应在要求律师亲自写订单前三思而行。

乔丹·罗斯曼是罗斯曼律师事务所的合伙人，该律所是一家全方位服务的纽约和新泽西律师事务所。他也是学生债务日记网站的创始人，该网站讨论了他如何偿还学生贷款。你可以通过电子邮件jordan@rothman.law联系乔丹。

这篇文章最初发布在Above the Law。
articles.summary:
One of the stranger practices I have encountered during my career is when judges decide motions at oral argument and then direct one of the lawyers to handwrite an order reflecting the court’s decision. This does not happen in every court, and plenty of judges either prepare their own orders or direct the parties to submit a proposed order after an appearance. However, I have seen judges announce a ruling and then expect counsel, sometimes right there in the courtroom, to write out an order that the judge can sign.

I understand why judges might employ this practice. Courts are busy, and it can be efficient to have the lawyers memorialize what just happened rather than requiring court personnel to prepare an order themselves. Moreover, the lawyers presumably understand the issues involved in a case and should be able to reduce a straightforward ruling to writing. Nevertheless, judges should generally avoid this practice since lawyers have adversarial interests, and handwritten orders prepared immediately after oral argument can create unnecessary confusion.

Perhaps the biggest problem is that lawyers may disagree about what the judge actually decided. Oral rulings are not always delivered with the precision of a written decision. A judge might discuss several issues, explain tentative thoughts, and then announce a ruling without specifying every detail necessary to implement that decision. The parties can walk away from the same oral argument with different understandings about exactly what relief was granted and what obligations the parties have going forward.

This can put lawyers in an awkward position when one attorney is asked to write the order. The lawyer naturally wants to draft language that is favorable to his or her client. Of course, attorneys have ethical obligations and should never intentionally misrepresent what a judge ruled. But there can be substantial room for reasonable disagreement about how an oral ruling should be reduced to writing. One lawyer might believe the judge intended a broad directive while opposing counsel believes the ruling was far narrower.

I once dealt with this situation after a judge decided a motion at oral argument and asked counsel to memorialize the ruling by hand. Almost immediately, there was disagreement among the lawyers about the language that should appear in the order. Everyone had just heard the same ruling, but the parties had different views about what the judge intended. Instead of ending the dispute, the ruling essentially created a new argument about how the ruling itself should be described.

Handwriting an order can create other problems as well. Lawyers are usually focused on advocating for their clients during oral argument, not taking a perfect transcription of everything the judge says. Counsel might be thinking about questions from the bench, arguments made by an adversary, or issues that need to be addressed before leaving the courtroom. Asking a lawyer moments later to reconstruct the precise contours of a ruling can therefore be a recipe for mistakes.

There is also something less than ideal about important judicial directives being memorialized through hurried handwriting in a courtroom. Depending on the circumstances, orders can affect discovery obligations, deadlines, monetary payments, injunctions, and numerous other significant rights. Lawyers and their clients may need to rely upon the exact wording of an order months or even years later. Everyone is better served when there is a clear document that accurately reflects what the court intended.

Of course, judges do not necessarily need to draft every order themselves. In many situations, it makes perfect sense for a judge to direct counsel to submit a proposed order after oral argument. This gives the parties time to review the language, consult a transcript if necessary, and identify disagreements before an order is entered. A judge can then resolve any disputes about wording and sign a document that accurately reflects the court’s ruling.

Judges could also dictate the precise terms of an order on the record or have court staff prepare a short order when the ruling is straightforward. Any of these approaches reduces the possibility that one side will have undue influence over the language simply because that lawyer happened to be holding the pen.

Lawyers already have enough things to fight about. They should not have to engage in a negotiation in the courtroom about what a judge meant five minutes earlier. When courts issue rulings, everyone benefits when the resulting orders are clear, deliberate, and unquestionably reflect the judge’s decision. Judges should therefore think twice before asking lawyers to write the order themselves.

Jordan Rothman is a partner of The Rothman Law Firm, a full-service New York and New Jersey law firm. He is also the founder of Student Debt Diaries, a website discussing how he paid off his student loans. You can reach Jordan through email at jordan@rothman.law.

The post Judges Should Not Make Lawyers Handwrite Orders After Oral Argument appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: The Viral Wachtell Kiss That Exposed A Bigger Biglaw Problem
articles.content:
编辑按：欢迎收看我们的每日栏目"今日名言"。

"在许多律所中，许多人虽然不赞成办公室恋情，但认为自己对此无能为力。同时也有强势的合伙人认为他们想做什么就能做什么。"
——咨询公司Zeughauser Group的合伙人彼得·泽乌豪瑟（Peter Zeughauser）在接受路透社采访时如此表示，评论的是大型律所办公室恋情问题，这一问题因Wachtell律所的一段亲密视频而被推向了风口浪尖。这段现在已病毒式传播的视频片段中，一位合伙人与一位助理律师在公开场合激吻，导致该合伙人失去了一次重要的跨所转职机会。

斯塔西·扎雷茨基（Staci Zaretsky）是《Above the Law》的主编，她从2011年开始在这里工作。她非常乐意听取您的意见，请随时给她发邮件分享任何线索、问题、评论或批评。您可以在Bluesky、X/Twitter和Threads上关注她，也可以在LinkedIn上与她联系。

（原文《病毒式传播的Wachtell亲吻事件揭示了大型律所的更大问题》首发于《Above the Law》）
articles.summary:
Ed. note: Welcome to our daily feature, Quote of the Day.

There are many people in firms who I think disapprove of [office romances] but don’t think there’s much they can do about it. And there are powerful partners ​who think they can do whatever they want.

— Peter Zeughauser, a partner at the Zeughauser Group consultancy, in comments given to Reuters, concerning Biglaw office romances in the wake of the Wachtell kiss seen round the world. That now viral video clip featured a partner and an associate engaged in a public makeout session, one that subsequently cost the partner a major lateral move.

Staci Zaretsky is the managing editor of Above the Law, where she’s worked since 2011. She’d love to hear from you, so please feel free to email her with any tips, questions, comments, or critiques. You can follow her on Bluesky, X/Twitter, and Threads, or connect with her on LinkedIn.
